title: Variables and Assignment
learningObjectives: Declare a local variable using an explicit C# type.
Use var when an initializer makes the inferred type clear.
Distinguish a variable's declared type from its current value.
Predict the value printed after a sequence of assignments.

understand.concept: A variable is a named local storage location whose value can change while a program runs. Every variable has a compile-time type. A declaration introduces the name and type; an initializer supplies an initial value; an assignment updates the value. Local variables must be definitely assigned before they are read.
understand.whyItMatters: Variables let programs retain information, calculate results and respond to changing data. Understanding declaration and assignment prevents type errors and accidental reads of uninitialized locals.
understand.analogy: A variable is like a labelled container: the label identifies the kind of value it can hold, while the contents may be replaced with another compatible value.
understand.analogyLimit: Unlike a physical container, a C# variable has a fixed compile-time type. Assigning a string to an int variable is not permitted just because the variable is being reused.

explain.narrative:
## Declaring a variable

Use a type followed by an identifier, optionally with an initializer. For example, an integer variable can be declared and initialized in one statement. The type determines which values and operations are valid.

## Assignment and reassignment

The assignment operator stores the value on its right in the variable on its left. It does not mean mathematical equality. A variable can be reassigned while the new value is compatible with its declared type.

## Explicit types and var

An explicit declaration states the type directly. The var keyword asks the compiler to infer a local variable's type from its initializer; it is still statically typed, not dynamically typed. var requires an initializer.

## Definite assignment

A local variable must receive a value on every execution path before it is read. Fields and properties have different default-initialization rules; do not transfer those rules to local variables.

## Version baseline

All examples use syntax supported by C# 14 and target .NET 10. var has been available since C# 3.0.
